lines: A single Parquet file, however well encoded and however skippable, is still just one immutable file.
ORC is the one real rival that made nearly every one of the same layout decisions differently.
Same data, two very different shapes. The question this topic answers is what that difference actually costs, and what it actually buys.
Neither format gets any special configuration here. ORC's own row index is built in, one entry for every ten thousand rows, always present.
Does that fixed index prune finer than Parquet's bare row-group statistics, by default, with nothing turned on?
answer: Yes. Parquet's row-group size is a choice the writer makes, and it's often set larger than ten thousand rows, so ORC's fixed, always-on index can prune finer with no configuration at all.
Watch what happens on a real selective query over the same hundred thousand rows.

lines: Inside an ORC stripe, each column is stored as several named streams, placed right next to each other in the file.
An ordinary integer column, for instance, becomes a present stream and a data stream.
Index streams always sit at the front of the stripe, so an ordinary scan never has to read them at all.
Here's the real measurement, on a hundred thousand rows. A selective query reads ten thousand rows under ORC's fixed row index.
The same query, under Parquet's bare row-group statistics at this row-group size, reads twenty-five thousand rows.
ORC's index needed no configuration to win that comparison.
steps.takeaway: ORC's row index needs no configuration — it prunes by default where Parquet's bare row-group stats are coarser.

lines: ORC's index is fixed at ten thousand rows, with nothing to configure. Does Parquet have any way to prune finer than that, once a writer turns something on?
answer: Yes. Parquet's own page index adds a second, finer layer of statistics inside each row group. It's opt-in, because that extra layer costs its own metadata.
Once it's turned on, it can out-prune ORC's fixed default.

lines: Turn Parquet's page index on, and the same query now reads only twenty-five hundred rows — finer than ORC's fixed default.
That precision isn't free. The page index costs four times as many metadata bytes as ORC's own row index.
All three measured together: ten thousand rows and two hundred index bytes for ORC. Twenty-five thousand rows and eighty index bytes for Parquet's bare row-group statistics.
Twenty-five hundred rows and eight hundred index bytes once Parquet's page index is switched on.
steps.takeaway: Finer pruning always costs more index bytes — ORC and Parquet just sit at different points on that trade-off.

lines: Now the history behind ORC's own name in Hive. Before the zero point thirteen release, Hive only guaranteed atomicity and durability at the partition level.
The zero point thirteen release added full row-level transactions, built so that any storage format with a row identifier could use them.
But the actual integration work was only ever done for ORC — which is exactly why ORC became Hive's own default.
So why did Parquet become the lakehouse-wide default anyway? Parquet was built from the start to be used by any framework, with no ecosystem favored over another.
And the table formats this chapter turns to next chose Parquet as their own default storage format.
ORC hasn't disappeared — it still runs in legacy Hive tables, and in some Trino estates that still read them.
steps.takeaway: ORC's own transactional history made it Hive's default; Parquet's framework-neutral design made it the lakehouse's.

lines: Step back, and here's the shape of it. ORC's fixed row index beats a bare row-group default, with nothing configured.
Parquet's own opt-in page index beats ORC's fixed default, once it's turned on.
And the wider ecosystem picked Parquet anyway — not because ORC's index lost, but because Parquet was built to belong to everyone.
